chapter: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
title: Strayhorn as meticulous genius behind Ellington
summary: Brown describes arrangements ordered by phone and says Strayhorn's richer writing is recognizable.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: I remember hearing him tell Duke that he had been playing, "Take the A Train" wrong. For a long, long time and he -- this was on a television show he did with Ralph Gleason he did for educational television, in San Francisco. And he played it the way, he said, "I wrote it, Edward," and he said "you haven't been playing it that way for a long time".

That's right, he was a very meticulous little fellow. And he was right in most everything he did. And many, many, many times Ellington would call him up from out on the road, "Sweetpea, I want an arrangement on so and so and so and so." Well, when do you need it? In a couple

of days, so -- and Sweetpea, "All right." And in a couple of days the most gorgeous arrangement on that particular piece. And that was Strayhorn and he never got the credit, I mean, he was always feeling that well, isn't that nice that this fellow took this little boy and give him such a nice chance? Oh, no, that's -- you're entirely wrong. He was the genius, the power behind that throne all of those latter years. He was terrific.
Yeah, I saw him do amazing things. A lot of people have said they can't tell Duke's writing from Strayhorn's. How about -- you're smiling.
Well that's because they never knew who wrote it.

I can because it's so much richer. You see, not taking anything away from anybody, age takes its toll. And the old, old, old people just had the common triads and notes and frame-ups like that, but the new better people they put tones in that made it so rich and beautiful. Beautified everything that was Strayhorn. I can tell you in a minute anything that was Strayhorn's. Now a whole lot of people took Strayhorn's work and learned how to play it like he wrote it, but that was Strayhorn.
